title: Free will
examples: Does everything that happens already have to happen?
If everything is determined, can we ever be truly responsible for our actions?
How can we have free will if physics suggests everything is predictable?

explain.say: Today we explore the big question of free will. You will learn about determinism first.

items: All actions are the result of prior causes

explain.say: Determinism suggests every event is fixed by what came before. Think about a rolling ball.

draw.text: Ball roll: Initial force dictates path.

explain.say: Free will is the idea that we can make genuine choices. You feel like you choose your own actions. This is the core idea.

draw.text: Free Will: Ability to choose otherwise.

explain.say: The conflict is between these two ideas. Can we be free if everything is caused? This is the main debate.
Compatibilism tries to solve this conflict. It suggests free will and determinism can both be true. You can be free within a determined system.
In real life, consider choosing your university major. You feel free, but your past influences your choice. This shows the tension.

draw.text: Real Life: Choosing a career path.

faq.q: If determinism is true, does it mean I cannot change my mind?
faq.a: No, determinism only says your current choice is caused by prior things. It does not mean you cannot change your mind if the causes change.
asks: Can I change my mind if everything is set?
Does determinism stop me from rethinking things?

faq.q: What exactly does compatibilism mean for my everyday life?
faq.a: It suggests that as long as your actions come from your own desires, you are free, even if those desires were ultimately caused.
asks: How does this affect my sense of personal choice?

faq.q: Is determinism a scientific fact or just a philosophical idea?
faq.a: It is primarily a philosophical position, though it draws heavily from physics. Science can describe causes, but philosophy debates the necessity of those causes.
asks: Is this idea based on science or just thought?

faq.q: Does free will require that my actions are completely random?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Some views argue that free will requires that the action is caused by me, even if that cause is itself determined.
asks: Must my choices be random to be free?
Is randomness the only way to be truly free?

faq.q: What is the biggest difference between determinism and libertarianism?
faq.a: Determinism says everything is caused. Libertarianism argues that some actions are uncaused by prior events, allowing true freedom.
asks: What is the opposite of determinism?
Which view says we can break the chain of cause?

facts: Determinism is the view that all events are ultimately determined by prior causes.
Free will is the capacity of agents to make genuine, uncoerced choices.
Compatibilism attempts to reconcile the concepts of free will and determinism.
A key debate involves whether our choices are fully predictable from the past.

quiz.say: If every event must have a prior cause, this view is called:
quiz.show: Which view holds that all events are caused?
quiz.why: Determinism directly claims that prior causes necessitate future events.

wrong.0: Random chance suggests no underlying cause, which is different from determinism.
wrong.2: This view suggests some actions are uncaused by prior events.
wrong.3: This view tries to make two ideas fit together, not state one absolute rule.

quiz.say: Which philosophical position suggests freedom exists even if causes exist?
quiz.show: Which view reconciles freedom and causation?
quiz.why: Compatibilism is defined by its attempt to show that free will and determinism can coexist.

wrong.0: Nihilism concerns meaning, not the causality of actions.
wrong.2: This view rejects free will entirely because of causation.
wrong.3: This is a general term for disagreeing, not a specific solution.

quiz.say: If I choose to study philosophy, and that choice was fully predictable from my upbringing, which concept is at play?
quiz.why: Predicting an action based on its preceding causes is the core idea of determinism.

wrong.0: This view implies the choice was not entirely fixed by the past.
wrong.1: While compatible, the question describes the prediction aspect, which is determinism.
wrong.2: Agency is the ability to act, not the description of the causal chain itself.
